title: Fixed and unalterable — but against what?
core: All three say a thing holds no matter what pressure is applied to it: it will not bend, break, or go away. The confusion is that each resists a *different* kind of pressure — the passage of time and circumstance, a deliberate attempt to find a gap, or an attempt to remove or hand over. They also live in different worlds: one belongs to nature and physical law, one to courtrooms and contracts, one to constitutions and declarations. Pick the wrong one and you claim the wrong kind of permanence.

words.nuance: Resists **change itself** — the thing has one nature and cannot take another, by anyone's hand. It's a metaphysical claim, not a legal one: laws of physics, the past, death. Note that nobody attacks an immutable thing; it simply isn't the kind of thing that varies. This is why it turns ironic so easily — call something immutable and reality can prove you wrong.

Resists **attack** — it presupposes an adversary hunting for the gap and failing to find one. That's why it attaches to alibis, contracts, guarantees, cases: things built by people to survive scrutiny. Unlike the others it's an assessment of workmanship, so it can be tested and can fail; and the only informal-register word here, at home in a newsroom or a boardroom.

Resists **transfer** — including by the holder. The unique force is that *you* cannot surrender it: no contract, sale, or waiver can move it off you, which is a limit on your own power, not just on others'. It attaches almost exclusively to rights, liberty, dignity — never to facts, alibis, or physical laws.

exam_note: Watch what the sentence says is being resisted: revision over time → immutable; scrutiny or loophole-hunting → ironclad; being taken, waived, or sold → inalienable. If the object is a right, inalienable is nearly always the intended answer; if the object is a fact or law of nature, ironclad is the trap.
